topic: Claude skills: what they are, how to install them safely, and how to make your own
audience: Professionals who use Claude every day and paste the same instructions again and again
goal: Install a skill they trust or one from Browse skills, then turn the instructions they paste most into their own first skill
notes: A skill is a small folder of instructions, and sometimes scripts and templates, that teaches Claude one job the way you want it done. You install it once; from then on Claude picks it up whenever a request needs it.

Every skill is a folder with one required file, SKILL.md. Its first lines hold a name, which is also the command you can type (such as /learn-anything), and a description of what the skill does and when to use it. Below that come the instructions: steps, rules, examples and checklists. A skill can also carry reference notes, templates and scripts.

Skills load in layers: always just the name and description of every skill you've switched on (a line or two each); the instructions when a request matches; extra files only if needed. Scripts run and only their results come back to Claude. That's why you can install many without slowing Claude down.

How skills compare: custom instructions are your general preferences and apply to every conversation; projects hold background documents and knowledge and apply to chats inside that project; connectors (MCP) give access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar, when Claude needs that app; a skill is a way of doing a particular job and applies only when a request needs it, in any chat. They work well together: a connector lets Claude reach your project tracker; a skill teaches it how your team writes tickets.
Skills follow an open standard, the Agent Skills specification (agentskills.io), so a skill you write isn't locked to one product.

Where skills work: Claude on the web and in the desktop app, on every plan from Free to Enterprise, once code execution is turned on; Claude Code, from folders on your computer (skills switched on in your Claude account also sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account); Claude for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook; Cowork, which uses the skills switched on for your account; the Claude API, in beta, through the code execution tool, where skills run in a sandbox with no internet access.

Install a skill in four steps: 1) get the skill's zip file and don't unzip it; 2) in Claude, open Settings → Capabilities and turn on Code execution and file creation (in the newer Settings layout it's called Create and edit files); 3) open Customize → Skills, click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill, and choose the zip; 4) check that the skill's switch is on, then ask for something the skill covers.
On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner must first turn them on in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab.

In Claude Code: for every project on your computer, unzip the skill into ~/.claude/skills/ (so you end up with ~/.claude/skills/learn-anything/SKILL.md); for one project and everyone who works on it, unzip it into the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it. Run it by typing a slash and its name, or just ask. /skills lists what's installed.

Using a skill: Claude reads the descriptions of your skills and uses one by itself when your request matches. To be sure, name it in your request, for example: 'Use my weekly-report skill on these notes.' In Claude Code and in the Microsoft 365 add-ins you can also type / and pick a skill from the list. If Claude doesn't use a skill you expected: check its switch is on, name it in your request, or make its description clearer about when it applies.
A skill is worth making once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times.

The parts of a skill, for example a weekly-report skill: weekly-report/SKILL.md (required: name, description and instructions), reference.md (optional: detail Claude reads only when it needs it), templates/ (optional: files to fill in), scripts/ (optional: code for steps that must be exact).

SKILL.md starts with its name and description between two lines of dashes, for example: name: weekly-report / description: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates.

Rules: the name uses lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, 64 characters at most, can't contain 'claude' or 'anthropic', and matches the folder's name. The description says what the skill does and when to use it, in the third person; Claude decides when to use the skill from this line alone; 200 characters at most in the Claude apps (the API allows 1,024); no tags in angle brackets. Instructions stay under 500 lines: numbered steps, the mistakes to avoid, one short example, and a checklist for long jobs. Link each extra file from SKILL.md and say when to read it. Use scripts for steps that must come out the same every time: calculations, format checks, conversions.
Package it: zip the folder, not the files inside it. The zip must contain weekly-report/SKILL.md. If the files sit at the top of the zip without their folder, the upload won't work.

Test it: write three requests that should use the skill and two that shouldn't; upload it, switch it on and try all five; if Claude misses one, improve the description first, because it's what Claude uses to choose.
On a Mac, Cowork can record you doing a task and propose a skill from it (on Pro, Max and Team plans).

Where to find more: Claude's own directory, in Customize → Skills → + → Browse skills, includes skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. Anthropic's examples on GitHub (github.com/anthropics/skills) are good to learn from and adapt.

Stay safe: a skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it, so treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. Install only from sources you trust; even a skill a colleague shares deserves a look first. Read every file before you switch a skill on, especially scripts, and look for anything that downloads software or sends information to a website. Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. The main risks are prompt injection (hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for) and data leaks. On Enterprise plans, owners can turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content.

The ten skills Mojeed wrote for the people he teaches, with a request to try for each: learn-anything (a patient tutor for any topic: asks what you know, makes a short plan, explains one idea at a time with an analogy and a small example, checks understanding; try: 'Teach me how neural networks learn. I know basic algebra.'); quiz-me (turns notes, a document or a topic into practice questions asked one at a time, explains every answer, comes back to what you miss; try: 'Quiz me on these lecture notes. Ten questions, mixed.'); research-brief (answers a question with a one-page, sourced brief, separates what's known from what's only claimed, gives each finding a confidence level, never invents a source); news-explainer (turns AI and tech news into a plain explainer: what happened, why it matters, who it affects and what's still unknown, every claim attributed, no hype; try: 'Explain this announcement for my newsletter readers.'); linkedin-post (LinkedIn posts in your own voice from an idea, a lesson or a piece of work: an opening worth reading, one clear point, no invented stories or engagement bait; try: 'Turn this project I finished into a post. Here are two of my old posts.'); job-application (tailors your CV and cover letter to a specific job ad, matches your real experience to what the employer asks for, tells you honestly where the gaps are; try: 'Here's my CV and the job ad. Tailor both.'); meeting-to-actions (turns meeting notes or a transcript into decisions, actions with owners and deadlines, open questions and a follow-up email, never invents an owner or a date; try: 'Here's the transcript of today's team call.'); presentation-planner (plans a talk before you open slide software: the story, one message per slide, titles that state the point, visuals and speaker notes; try: 'Plan a ten-minute talk on our quarterly results for the board.'); check-the-numbers (answers questions about spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL results and proves the answer first: a script profiles each file for missing values, numbers stored as text, repeated rows and keys, and gaps in the dates; every join is checked for multiplied rows; try: 'Which products drove last quarter's revenue? Here's the export.'); skill-maker (interviews you about a task you repeat, writes the SKILL.md, checks it against the rules and packages the folder as a zip ready to upload; try: 'Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill.').
Mojeed's website: https://mojeedabisiga.com/ (his biography, work, speaking and contact).
